concepts.def: Pathway by which a chemical element moves through biotic and abiotic compartments of Earth.
Compartment storing a quantity of an element, e.g., ocean carbon, soil nitrogen.
Average time an element spends in a reservoir = reservoir size / flux.
Slow, sedimentary cycle: weathering of rocks releases phosphate; runs through life and back to ocean sediments.

walkthroughs.body_html:
The Physical Environment — a core area of A-Level Environmental Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Physical Environment brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Physical Environment.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which cycle has no significant atmospheric phase?
options: Carbon
Nitrogen
Phosphorus
Sulfur

mcqs.q: Average time in a reservoir is called?
options: Flux
Residence time
Lifetime
Half-life

mcqs.q: How are most microplastics formed in the environment?
options: Bacteria produce them.
Larger plastic items break down physically into smaller fragments over time.
They are all manufactured at microscopic size deliberately.
Forest fires alone.

mcqs.q: What is the leading driver of global deforestation?
options: Rainforests are deserts most of the year.
Logging for timber and paper.
Agriculture (especially cattle ranching, soy, palm oil).
Forest fires alone.

mcqs.q: Why are tropical rainforest soils often nutrient-poor despite abundant vegetation?
options: Rainforests are deserts most of the year.
Rainforests have rich soils because they are productive.
Bacteria produce them.
Rapid decomposition and uptake mean nutrients cycle quickly through living biomass, not soil.

Compartment storing a quantity of an element, e.g., ocean carbon, soil nitrogen.

Average time an element spends in a reservoir = reservoir size / flux.
